text: By the early 1950s the restrictive covenants were gone, struck down by the Supreme Court a few years earlier, and Black families were moving into the blocks around the University of Chicago.
The campus sat in the middle of a neighborhood that was changing block by block, and the people who ran the university were afraid.
They were afraid the campus would end up stranded, an island of stone buildings surrounded by a place its faculty wouldn't live and its trustees didn't recognize.
So the university decided it would not wait to see what happened.
It would rebuild the neighborhood itself.
What happened over the next decade made Hyde Park the most studied case of urban renewal in the country, and a template other universities copied.
It is also the place where the gap between the words and the outcome is easiest to measure.

In 1952, after a sensational kidnapping and assault case and a reported thirty-two percent jump in crime over three years, the university called a mass meeting and stood up a new organization called the South East Chicago Commission.
Its stated mission was to drive crime and corruption from the neighborhood.
The real engine was its executive director, a corporate lawyer named Julian Levi, brother of the law school's dean.
Levi ran the commission for nearly thirty years, and he ran it hard.
